podcast.title: Sex Pistols Contract (1977)
podcast.body: The Sex Pistols signed their contract with Virgin Records on March 10, 1977, in front of Buckingham Palace, an event that "kicked punk into high gear in the UK." "The sex pistol signing their Virgin Records contract in front of Buckingham Palace on March 10th, 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Signing (1977)
podcast.body: In 1977, after EMI and A&M Records dropped the Sex Pistols due to their controversial nature, Richard Branson seized the opportunity to sign them. This "smart move" capitalized on the punk explosion and led to a string of New Wave and Post-Punk hits for Virgin. "Branson though saw an opportunity and signed them up. Smart move."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Third Label for Sex Pistols (1977)
podcast.body: In May 1977, the Sex Pistols signed with Virgin Records, becoming their third label. "In May of 1977, the pistols signed with their third label, Virgin Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 4

podcast.title: Expansion into Other Areas & Sale to EMI (1992)
podcast.body: Thanks to its musical success, Virgin diversified into other business areas. Branson eventually sold the company to EMI for approximately a billion dollars in 1992, using the funds to finance the creation of Virgin Airlines. "Thanks to music, Virgin expanded into other areas before Branson sold the company to EMI for about a billion dollars in 1992. And that's how he managed to finance the creation of Virgin Airlines."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Refusal of Tour Support for PiL (1992)
podcast.body: Virgin Records refused to provide further tour support for Public Image Limited, which directly led to the band's last gig on September 18, 1992, and subsequent breakup. "It became their last show when their label, Virgin Records, refused to pay for any more tour support, so that was it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Support for Online Music (1996)
podcast.body: Virgin Records supported David Bowie's decision to make his song "Telling Lies" available for download in 1996, seeing him as the perfect test bed for this new digital distribution method. "In 1996, he made a song available for download with the support of his label Virgin Records, who also saw where things were going."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 3

podcast.title: Contractual Obligations
podcast.body: Public Image Ltd created the song "Fodderstompf" as a "joke" to fulfill minimum duration requirements specified in their contract with Virgin Records for their debut album. "cumplir con la adoración mínima que segiar contra lo que tenían con Virgén."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Deal Review and Reunion Suggestion
podcast.body: Iggy Pop's deal with Virgin Records was under review, and his next record needed to generate significant buzz to prevent him from being dropped. It was "quietly suggested" that Iggy round up guest musicians, specifically hinting at the "Ashton Boys," for an album which eventually became *Skull Ring*. "Iggy's deal with Virgin Records was under review. The next record had to generate some buzz, or he would be dropped."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Doubts on Music Response Commercial Viability
podcast.body: As the record label responsible for The Chemical Brothers, Virgin Records held considerable reservations regarding the commercial viability of "Music Response" as a single. Despite the song's popularity and recognized quality, the label questioned its potential for mainstream success. "tenían bastantes dudas y hasta que punto era una canción suficientemente comercial para compartir el Singer."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Music Response y el single gafado

podcast.title: Expansion to Retail Store (Age 22)
podcast.body: At 22, Branson expanded his venture into a small retail store named "Virgin Records and Tapes" located in the Notting Hill area of London. "When he was 22, the venture expanded to a small store called Virgin Records and Tapes in the Notting Hill area of London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Financial Support for Sid Vicious's Legal Defense
podcast.body: Virgin Records paid all of Sid Vicious's legal costs following his charge for Nancy Spungin's murder. The label also reportedly paid $20,000 in royalty money to Sid, which was allegedly stolen from his Chelsea Hotel room the night Nancy died. "All the legal costs were paid by Virgin Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: First Major Hit (Tubular Bells)
podcast.body: Virgin's first signing was Mike Oldfield's "Tubular Bells," which became a huge hit and provided the financial resources for the company's expansion. "So Branson and his partners did, and their first signing was 2-biter bells by Mike Oldfield. That became a huge hit which allowed Virgin to finance an expansion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Founding and Early Success
podcast.body: Virgin Records was founded by Richard Branson in the early 1970s. The label achieved its initial and significant financial success primarily through the release of Michael Field's "Tubular Bells" in 1973, which generated substantial profits and propelled Virgin towards becoming the large multinational corporation it eventually became. "Richard Branson empezó su discográfica justo a primeros de los 70 y tubular bells fue el gran éxito que lo hizo ganar muchísimo dinero."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Mike Oldfield - Amarok. ¿Es su mejor disco?

podcast.title: Founding as Mail-Order Service (Age 15)
podcast.body: Richard Branson started Virgin at the age of 15 as a mail-order record service and fanzine, operating out of his bedroom. "Richard Branson started Virgin when he was just 15. His first incarnation was a male-order record service and fan scene from his bedroom."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: God Save the Queen Pressing Issues
podcast.body: The Virgin Label encountered significant difficulties in getting the Sex Pistols' "God Save the Queen" pressed. This was primarily because some workers at the manufacturing plant were so deeply offended by the song's content that they refused to perform their duties. "Virgin had a very hard time getting this record pressed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 5

podcast.title: Iggy Pop's Contract Review
podcast.body: Iggy Pop's recording contract with Virgin Records was under review, requiring his next album to generate "some buzz" to avoid being dropped, which led to a suggestion for him to collaborate with the Ashton brothers of The Stooges. "Iggy's deal with Virgin Records was under review. The next record had to generate some buzz or he would be dropped."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Missing Royalties – After Nancy Spungen's Death
podcast.body: Following Nancy Spungen's death, a significant sum of money, estimated by some at $20,000 in royalties from Virgin Records, was reported missing from her and Sid's hotel room. This led to speculation about a robbery as a motive for her murder. "Others say $20,000 in royalties from Virgin Records, was missing for the room."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sid Vicious

podcast.title: Pressure on Michael Field
podcast.body: Virgin Records exerted considerable pressure on Michael Field over several years, specifically pushing for the creation of a "Tubular Bells 2." This persistent demand was a major factor contributing to Michael Field's growing dissatisfaction with the label and his subsequent decision to release "Amarok" as a commercially unviable project. "Virging llevaba muchos años presionando a Michael Field para hacer el tubular verse 2."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Mike Oldfield - Amarok. ¿Es su mejor disco?

podcast.title: Pushing for "Don't You Want Me" Release
podcast.body: The Human League's label, Virgin, insisted on releasing "Don't You Want Me" as a single despite frontman Phil Oakey considering it "filler" and "NAF." They "doubled down" by commissioning the band's most expensive music video, a meta-film noir. "Oki thought the song was filler, he called it NAF, and he tried to dissuade his label, Virgin, from putting it out as a 45."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: The British Are Charting Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: The British Are Charting Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Relationship with Michael Field
podcast.body: Michael Field expressed significant discontent with his tenure at Virgin Records, openly criticizing both the label and Richard Branson in numerous interviews. He believed that Virgin's involvement played a "quite bad role" and potentially impacted the quality of his discography during the 1980s, despite his work during that period being considered very good. "estaba ya muy descontento con su tapa con Virging Records, me refiero a bastantes entrevistas en las que la habla francamente mal, tanto de Richard Ranson como de Virging Records."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Mike Oldfield - Amarok. ¿Es su mejor disco?

podcast.title: Role in Techno's European Introduction
podcast.body: Virgin Records played a pivotal role in introducing Detroit techno to a European audience through a curated compilation album. Talent scout Neil Rushton initiated contact with Derrick May to explore the Detroit scene, leading to the landmark release "Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit." "El Caza Talentos de Virgin Records, Neil Raeston, se opuso un contacto con Derrick May, con el objetivo de descubrir más sobre la escena de Detroit."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Cómo Detroit Reinventó la Música Electrónica ｜ Pioneros del Techno

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Single Release
podcast.body: Virgin Records released the Sex Pistols' 7-inch single "Pretty Vacant" in 1977, carrying the serial number VS184. "It's the original release on Virgin Records, 1977, and carries the serial number of VS184."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Your questions answered

podcast.title: Sex Pistols' Enduring Deal
podcast.body: The Sex Pistols' third record deal was with Virgin Records, and this particular contract proved to be successful, allowing the band to achieve significant sensation and disrupt the British establishment.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock

podcast.title: Signing of Krautrock Bands
podcast.body: Virgin Records was among British labels that actively signed Krautrock bands, perceiving their music as another form of progressive rock. This move played a crucial role in introducing Krautrock to the UK and its subsequent influence on post-punk music. "Virgin Records and one or two other labels signed up pretty much every crop rock band that they found, considering it to be another form of proc rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Explaining Krautrock

podcast.title: Simple Minds and "Don't You (Forget About Me)"
podcast.body: When composer Keith Forsey was struggling to find an artist for "Don't You (Forget About Me)" for *The Breakfast Club* soundtrack, he turned to Virgin Records for suggestions. Virgin suggested Simple Minds, despite the band's initial reluctance to record an outsider's song, ultimately leading to their biggest hit. "So in desperation, Keith Forsy turned to Virgin Records. Have you got anyone you think could do this on justice? Virgin had a listen, gave it a thing and said, well, how about simple minds?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Key Alt-Rock Movie Soundtracks

podcast.title: Transition to Record Label (Post-Distribution)
podcast.body: Initially, Virgin distributed imports for other labels rather than signing artists directly. Later, Branson and his partners decided to establish their own label. "The company didn't sign any artist directly, what they did was distribute imports for other labels. But after a while, why not start a new label?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1
